title: All I Do Is in the Cause of Glory
intro: Al-Batalyawsi says al-Ma'arri addressed a Syrian host who had treated him badly and cast doubt on his beliefs. He turns the charges against him into a list of virtues, then lets a dim star accuse the sun of being hard to see. A night ride carries that reversal into the landscape, where a black horse becomes a second night beneath the first. The poem ends by asking what further rise is possible for a moon already full.

translation: All I do is in the cause of glory,
restraint, courage, sound judgement and an open hand.
1.sharh: He gives glory a practical definition. Two qualities govern what he holds back or risks, and two govern what he decides and what he gives away.

translation: Here with me, after all the secrets I have fathomed,
could a slanderer win belief or a petitioner go away empty?
2.sharh: The two visitors want different things from him. Experience lets him see through the informer, while generosity prevents him turning away someone in need.

translation: The least my coldness means is that I detest you.
The mildest form my estrangement takes is leaving.
3.sharh: The paired words “least” and “mildest” leave the more severe possibilities unspoken. What begins as a feeling in the first half becomes a departure in the second.

translation: Once a crosswind blows between me and you,
the last thing that weighs with me is what the reproachers say.
4.sharh: The wind blowing across the usual directions gives their relation a physical disturbance. The conventional voices urging a lover to stay have little hold on this departing guest.

translation: Some people count my sins as many.
My only offences are high aims and generous deeds.
5.sharh: He accepts his accusers' arithmetic and disputes the entries in their ledger. Each offence, once described in his own terms, is something he can take pride in.

translation: As though, when I outstripped the age and its people,
I came back owing humankind a debt of blood.
6.sharh: The slightly different forms sounded at the centre and the end link superiority with blood claims. Their resentment is so intense that he might have killed their relations.

translation: My name has travelled through the lands. Who could help them
hide a sun whose light is at its full?
7.sharh: His fame has done the travelling on its own. The image changes the labour involved in suppressing a name into that of screening a whole sun.

translation: Part of what I keep within would trouble the nights.
Less than what I carry would weigh Mount Radwa down.
8.sharh: He reveals the weight of his concerns while keeping their contents private. Even time itself and a mountain would have difficulty with a fraction of his load.

translation: Though I have come last in time,
I shall bring what my predecessors could never achieve.
9.sharh: The concession concerns the calendar. He treats the achievement of earlier generations as an open challenge, and the future tense leaves his own answer still to come.

translation: I set out at dawn though morning be swords,
and travel by night though darkness be armies.
10.sharh: The brightness of drawn blades and the mass of a host furnish dangers proper to the two times of day. He keeps travelling through either.

translation: I am a thoroughbred whose bridle has never been adorned,
a Yemeni blade the polishers overlooked.
11.sharh: The unadorned bridle and unpolished blade move the argument from other people's judgement to the outward signs on which they base it. Both objects already possess their worth.

translation: If a man's distinction lies in what he wears,
the sword consists of its scabbard and straps.
12.sharh: The sword disappears inside the definition. All that remains of it under the proposed test is the equipment that clothes or carries it.

translation: I have a voice that will not let me rest at my station,
though I have come to lodge between the two Simaks.
13.sharh: His power of speech takes on a will of its own. Even a lodging measured out between two of the brightest stars fails to satisfy it.

translation: I dwell where every lord longs to be
and the hand that reaches for it falls short.
14.sharh: A hand stretching upwards translates the social ambition into a bodily movement. It is easy to look up at his station and impossible, he says, to touch it.

translation: When I saw ignorance spreading among people,
I played the ignorant till they thought I really was.
15.sharh: The middle verb describes a deliberate performance. The people who see him perform remove that distinction and give him the simple name “ignorant”.

translation: What a wonder, how many who lack merit claim it.
What grief, how often someone of merit makes a show of lack.
16.sharh: The pretender and the accomplished person both produce a false public impression. His own decision to play ignorant now becomes part of a wider loss.

translation: How can the birds sleep in their nests
when snares have been set for the two stars by the pole?
17.sharh: The two stars sit beyond the reach of any birdcatcher. An outrage aimed that high makes the little distance between a nest and the earth feel like scant protection.

translation: Yesterday vies with today for the honour of my company.
My evenings envy the hours I spend before dawn.
18.sharh: Yesterday begrudges today the poet it has lost. Rivalry draws closer when late afternoon envies the hours before dawn, though both can claim his company in the course of a single day.

translation: Long have I known time and its sudden turns.
I no longer mind whom calamities carry off.
19.sharh: Familiarity with time has hardened into a startling indifference. The next verse will test the boast on a loss closer than anyone else's.

translation: Were my upper arm torn away, my shoulder would not grieve.
Were my forearm to die, my fingertips would not weep.
20.sharh: He chooses parts attached to one another. Each is imagined surviving its neighbour with the same unnatural composure he claims towards the world.

translation: When Madir calls the man of Tayy a miser
and Baqil taunts Quss with being tongue-tied,
21.sharh: Four proverbial figures make two inverted judgements. The habitual miser passes sentence on generosity, and the man who could scarcely answer a question judges an orator.

translation: and Suha says to the sun, “You are hard to see”,
and darkness says, “Dawn, your colour has faded”,
22.sharh: The tiny star normally tests the observer's own eyesight. Giving it the power to fault the sun makes more palpable the arrogance of judging a quality one lacks.

translation: and earth foolishly measures its height against the sky,
and pebbles and boulders boast against the stars,
23.sharh: The stones do the boasting. Arabic names the stars first, then reveals the lowly pebbles and rocks that have made themselves the stars' rivals.

translation: then come to me, death, for life is contemptible.
Be in earnest, my soul, for your age is at play.
24.sharh: Three verses of suspended syntax end in a double summons. He welcomes death into such a world, then asks his own soul to keep faith with seriousness while it lives.

translation: Often I set out while night weeps in sorrow
for itself, and the stars lean west.
25.sharh: The dew makes night appear to mourn its own departure. The westward lean of the stars tells the rider where he is in the passage towards dawn.

translation: I ride a wind lent a hoof of chrysolite,
her body gold, her anklets silver.
26.sharh: A horse takes shape out of wind. The gold gives her body its colour, and the silver round her lower legs describes pale markings in the form of jewellery.

translation: As though the east wind had thrown me its reins,
she trots with my saddle, then deftly changes step.
27.sharh: The rein gives wind a point at which the rider can touch it. The shifting movement beneath his saddle makes the praise of speed into an account of two gaits.

translation: When the horses long for watering places, she turns
from the water, and the watering places long for her.
28.sharh: A thirsty animal's need becomes a pool's desire. The repeated Arabic word for watering places has changed from the object of longing to its subject.

translation: Two nights, one with stars adorning its middle,
the other bare of all the stars' jewellery.
29.sharh: One darkness is overhead and one beneath the rider, his dark mount. Ornaments distinguish the two, as the silver on the earlier horse did. They are not two successive nights.

translation: Its darkness is separation, morning a promise
of meeting, and first light a lover who keeps me waiting.
30.sharh: The first glimmer is only a promise. The impatience of a lover explains how the rider can see the signs of dawn and still feel that it will never come.

translation: On him I crossed a sea whose swell surged high,
with no shore to it save the breaking light.
31.sharh: Al-Tabrizi considers a desert likened to the sea, then prefers the night itself. A shore made of daybreak gives the reader a way to decide between the two.

translation: Deep in each place of dread I have the company
of a night traveller whose ways have never sobered.
32.sharh: His companion is the night. The word for coming to one's senses invites the idea of a drunken gait, and the next verses make the companion's slow, unsteady progress visible.

translation: A middle-aged man of the Zanj, his parting gone grey,
bound so tightly he can scarcely rise.
33.sharh: The simile uses the dark complexion of a man from the East African coast. Stars supply the grey in his hair, and his imagined bonds express the traveller's long wait for night to lift.

translation: The Pleiades, with morning at their heels, seem
a man stumbling, or a limping man forcing himself on.
34.sharh: Daylight ought to frighten the cluster into flight. Instead the stars labour across the sky with the effort of a stumbling traveller trying to put weight on a lame leg.

translation: Once good fortune is granted you, you need not care,
even if the tribes glare sideways at you.
35.sharh: The address opens out to anyone favoured by fortune. Success now has a force of its own, capable of overriding the hostile intentions in other people's sidelong looks.

translation: The spears on their champions' shoulders take care to avoid you.
Blades fear you inside their scabbards.
36.sharh: Hostility belongs to the armed men, but their weapons have acquired wills of their own. Even the swords still safely sheathed feel fear.

translation: Should enemies aim their arrows towards you,
the broadheads recoil upon their own nocks.
37.sharh: The broad metal point and the little notch for the string belong at opposite ends. His fortune makes a threat reverse its ordinary direction.

translation: Calamities spare every padded foot and toe,
while humps and withers meet their death at their hands.
38.sharh: All the parts belong to one camel. What stands highest is most exposed, the first hint that the elevation he has been claiming carries its own dangers.

translation: The butts of spears come back intact,
their forward shafts smashed against men in mail.
39.sharh: The contrast is now within one weapon. Its leading length bears the damage, while the end furthest from the point of impact survives intact.

translation: If you seek honour, seek a middle station.
At the utmost reach, the man who stretches comes up short.
40.sharh: He is the same speaker whose ambition outgrew two stars. Position looks different when seen from the point beyond which another upward step is impossible.

translation: Full moons escape all loss while they are crescents.
Their waning overtakes them when they are complete.
41.sharh: A crescent can change by gaining light. Once the disc is full, its next change must be a loss. The advice about where to stop becomes something a reader can see.

1.2.1.head: عَفاف
1.2.1.meaning: Self-restraint, particularly in what one covets or might take.

1.2.3.head: حَزم
1.2.3.meaning: Sound judgement, with the consequences of action in view.

1.2.4.head: نائِل
1.2.4.meaning: Generosity, literally the gift that reaches a petitioner.

2.1.3.head: مارَسَ
2.1.3.meaning: Grappled with something repeatedly and came to know it from experience.

2.2.2.meaning: A talebearer, someone carrying reports to turn people against one another.

3.1.2.head: صُدود
3.1.2.meaning: Turning away, including the withdrawal of affection.

4.1.3.head: النَّكباء
4.1.3.meaning: A crosswind blowing between two recognised wind directions. It marks a falling-out.

4.2.5.head: عاذِلَة
4.2.5.meaning: Women who reproach a lover or try to turn someone from a departure.

5.2.5.meaning: High distinction, the very thing his enemies hold against him.

5.2.6.head: فاضِلَة
5.2.6.meaning: Excellences and generous services one renders others.

6.1.3.head: طالَ
6.1.3.meaning: Surpassed, got the better of someone in a contest of worth.

6.2.4.head: طائِلَة
6.2.4.meaning: Outstanding claims for blood or vengeance. It echoes the sound of “outstripped”.

7.2.4.head: مُتَكامِل
7.2.4.meaning: At full strength, as he claims his reputation is.

8.1.6.head: مُضمِر
8.1.6.meaning: Harbouring something within, whether a care or a purpose.

8.2.2.meaning: Radwa, a mountain near Yanbu in the Hijaz, proverbial for its weight and solidity.

9.1.4-5.head: الأَخير زَمانُه
9.1.4-5.meaning: “The one whose time is last”, the most recent in date among those being compared.

9.2.5.head: الأَوائِل
9.2.5.meaning: Those who came first, earlier generations whose achievements carry authority.

10.1.5.head: صارِم
10.1.5.meaning: Sharp blades, imagined in the white light of morning.

10.2.1.head: أَسرى
10.2.1.meaning: I journey by night, paired with setting out early in the morning.

10.2.5.head: جَحفَل
10.2.5.meaning: Massed armies, suggesting the density of the dark.

11.1.4-5.head: حَلّى اللِّجام
11.1.4-5.meaning: To adorn a bridle. Commentators also consider the sense of unfastening one.

11.2.1.head: نِضو
11.2.1.meaning: A bare blade, or one still awaiting the finishing work of a sword-polisher.

11.2.2.meaning: Yemeni, an origin traditionally associated with fine sword blades.

11.2.4.head: صَيقَل
11.2.4.meaning: Sword-polishers, the craftspeople who give a blade its finished surface.

12.2.4.head: غِمد
12.2.4.meaning: The sheath that encloses a blade.

12.2.5.head: حَمائِل
12.2.5.meaning: The belts or straps by which a sword is suspended.

13.1.2.head: مَنطِق
13.1.2.meaning: Eloquence, the power of articulate speech that secures his standing.

13.1.6.head: كُنه
13.1.6.meaning: The true extent or limit of something, here his present station.

13.2.4.head: السِّماكان
13.2.4.meaning: The two Simaks, the stars Arcturus and Spica, evoked for their height.

14.2.4.head: المُتَناوِل
14.2.4.meaning: Someone reaching out a hand towards what they can see.

15.2.1.head: تَجاهَلَ
15.2.1.meaning: Feigned ignorance, consciously imitating the people around him.

16.1.5.head: الفَضل
16.1.5.meaning: Merit, the quality that gives a person distinction.

16.2.1-2.head: وا أَسَفاً
16.2.1-2.meaning: “Alas for it”, a cry of grief at seeing someone hide their real worth.

17.1.5.head: وُكنَة
17.1.5.meaning: Roosts or nests where birds settle for the night.

17.2.3.head: الفَرقَدان
17.2.3.meaning: Al-Farqadan, Kochab and Pherkad in Ursa Minor, two stars near the north celestial pole.

18.2.2.head: سَحَر
18.2.2.meaning: The final hours of darkness just before dawn.

18.2.4.head: أَصيل
18.2.4.meaning: Late afternoons, the answering end of the day.

19.1.2.head: اِعتِراف
19.1.2.meaning: Long acquaintance or recognition through experience.

19.2.4-5.head: غالَ
19.2.4-5.meaning: Calamities carry someone off. Verb and noun share a root associated with destruction by surprise.

20.2.3.head: زَند
20.2.3.meaning: The forearm bone towards the wrist.

20.2.6.head: أُنمُلَة
20.2.6.meaning: Fingertips, imagined as capable of weeping.

21.1.3.head: الطّائِيّ
21.1.3.meaning: Al-Ta'i, Hatim of the tribe of Tayy, proverbial for hospitality and open-handedness.

21.1.5.head: مادِر
21.1.5.meaning: Madir, a man of Banu Hilal proverbial for miserliness. The recording has the consonants reversed, Marid. The name in the proverb is Madir.

21.2.2.head: قُسّ
21.2.2.meaning: Quss ibn Sa'ida, remembered as an eloquent Arab orator.

21.2.3.head: الفَهاهَة
21.2.3.meaning: Inarticulacy, the inability to express oneself clearly.

21.2.4.head: باقِل
21.2.4.meaning: Baqil, a proverbial figure of speechlessness who here presumes to judge an orator.

22.1.2.meaning: Al-Suha, the faint star Alcor beside Mizar. Picking it out was a test of eyesight.

22.2.6.head: حائِل
22.2.6.meaning: Changed for the worse, faded in colour.

23.1.1.head: طاوَلَ
23.1.1.meaning: Tried to rival another in height or stature.

23.2.2.head: شُهب
23.2.2.meaning: Bright stars that the stones claim to rival.

23.2.4.head: جَندَل
23.2.4.meaning: Large rocks or boulders, paired with little pebbles.

24.2.3.meaning: Be in earnest, the instruction he gives his own soul.

25.1.2.head: اِغتَدى
25.1.2.meaning: Set off early in the day.

25.1.3-4.head: بُكاء اللَّيل
25.1.3-4.meaning: “Night weeps”, the dew figured as tears at night's approaching end.

26.1.5.head: زَبَرجَد
26.1.5.meaning: Chrysolite, a green gemstone suggesting both colour and hardness.

26.2.2.head: التِّبر
26.2.2.meaning: Native or unworked gold, supplying the colour of the horse's body.

26.2.4.head: اللُّجَين
26.2.4.meaning: Silver, the colour circling the lower legs like anklets.

27.1.2.meaning: Al-saba, the east wind, whose speed the rider feels in his mount.

27.1.5.head: عِنان
27.1.5.meaning: Rein, the strap through which the rider guides a horse.

27.2.4.head: ناقَلَ
27.2.4.meaning: Places its feet deftly in succession, changing step with precision.

28.1.4.head: مَنهَل
28.1.4.meaning: Watering places reached by travellers and their mounts.

29.1.2.meaning: Adorned or wearing jewellery. Its opposite comes at the rhyme.

29.1.4.head: جَوز
29.1.4.meaning: Its middle or midst, here studded with stars.

29.2.5.head: عاطِل
29.2.5.meaning: Bare of ornaments, the starless darkness of the horse's coat.

30.2.4-5.head: حِبّ مُماطِل
30.2.4-5.meaning: “A lover who puts you off”, one who keeps postponing a promised meeting.

31.1.4-5.head: عَبَّ عُبابُ البَحر
31.1.4-5.meaning: “Its swell surges”, a repeated sound for waves rising and churning.

31.2.4.head: التَّبَلُّج
31.2.4.meaning: The breaking of day as darkness gives way.

32.1.5.head: مَخوفَة
32.1.5.meaning: A feared place or dangerous stretch of open country.

32.2.1-2.head: حَليف سُرى
32.2.1-2.meaning: “Companion of night travel”, a way of making night itself the traveller's familiar.

32.2.4.head: صَحا
32.2.4.meaning: Sober up or come round. The night has a drunkard's unsteady ways.

33.1.2.head: الزِّنج
33.1.2.meaning: Zanj, a historical Arabic designation for peoples of the East African coast.

33.1.5.head: مَفرِق
33.1.5.meaning: The parting in the hair, where the first grey stands out.

33.2.1.head: أَوثَقَ
33.2.1.meaning: Was bound or fettered, so that rising is an effort.

34.1.2.meaning: Al-Thurayya, the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus.

34.1.4.head: راعَ
34.1.4.meaning: Frightens the Pleiades. The commentaries describe their alarm at daybreak. The middle consonant is unclear in this recording.

34.2.4.head: ظالِع
34.2.4.meaning: Limping, especially from pain while still attempting to walk.

35.1.5-6.head: لم تُبَل
35.1.5-6.meaning: You need not care, a contracted form of the usual verb.

36.1.1.head: اِتَّقى
36.1.1.meaning: Avoided you or stood in fear of you. The spears are the subject.

37.2.1.head: نَكَصَ
37.2.1.meaning: Drew back or went into reverse.

37.2.3.head: فوق
37.2.3.meaning: Nocks, the notches at the back of arrows that take the bowstring.

37.2.4.head: مِعبَلَة
37.2.4.meaning: Broad, long arrowheads, here standing for the arrows tipped with them.

38.1.5.head: مَنسِم
38.1.5.meaning: A camel's toenail at the front of its padded foot.

38.2.3-4.head: الذُّرى وَالكَواهِل
38.2.3-4.meaning: Humps and withers, the prominent upper parts of a camel.

39.1.2.head: عَقِب
39.1.2.meaning: The butts of spears, furthest from the spearheads.

39.2.4.head: دارِع
39.2.4.meaning: Men in armour, whose mail takes the impact.

39.2.5.head: عامِل الرُّمح
39.2.5.meaning: The forward portions of the shafts just below the metal points.

40.1.6.head: تَوَسُّط
40.1.6.meaning: A middle position below the utmost height.

40.2.2.meaning: Reaching the extreme limit beyond which there is no room.

41.1.1.meaning: Avoid a loss, while the moon is still on the increase.

41.2.4.head: كامِلَة
41.2.4.meaning: Full, with the disc entirely illuminated.
